Numerical and graphical methods of descriptive statistics are introduced. Data analytic methods are demonstrated using the statistical computing software R.

parse_number()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Counting







count()


This function gives a quick tally of how many rows have each value. Add sort = TRUE to see the biggest groups first.












count() is a shortcut. The long way lets you compute extra summaries in the same step:















n() only works inside dplyr verbs


n() returns the size of the current group. Outside of summarize(), mutate(), or filter(), there is no “current group”, so it fails. - i.e. survey |> n(program) doesn’t mean anything.

text:
Recycling Vectors
When two vectors have different lengths, R recycles the shorter one by repeating it. That can quietly give wrong answers. Are the students in Arts or Business?















Doesn’t give you an error, just the wrong answer


R compares program with "Arts", "Business", "Arts", "Business", ... row by row. It does not ask “is the program Arts or Business?”. You only get about half of the students.




The fix is %in%, which you’ve seen in last lecture:

Maximum and Minimum

pmin() and pmax() work row by row across vectors (the “p” is for parallel)
min() and max() summarize everything into one value
















Key idea


Every row gets the same answer from min() and max(): the smallest and largest value in both columns combined. Use pmin() and pmax() for a per-row answer.

Time: Hours and minutes







Modular Arithmetic


Division with a quotient and a remainder: - %/% is integer division - %% is the remainder - E.g. 7%/%3=2 and 7%%3=1.












sleep_hours = 6.7 means 6 hours and 42 minutes. Modular arithmetic splits it:

Rounding







round(x)


This function rounds to the nearest integer. You can even add a digits argument that controls where to round, and this value digits can be negative!












Grades rounded to the nearest ten:















Always round down or up?


floor() always rounds down and ceiling() always rounds up. See the appendix.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Cutting numbers into ranges







cut()


This function chops a numeric vector into bins and returns a factor. You supply the break points. Give labels one fewer element than breaks.



















Open-ended bins



Values outside the breaks become NA. Use -Inf and Inf as the outer breaks so nothing falls off the ends.
Bins are right-closed by default, like (5, 10]. Pass right = FALSE to make them left-closed, like [5, 10).

min_rank()


This function gives the rank of each value. 1 is the smallest, unless you flip it with desc().

Summaries: mean or median?








Why are they so different? Look at the distribution:















Perhaps an explanation


Many students do not work at all, which drags the median down while a few heavy workers pull the mean up. When a distribution is skewed, maybe it’s worth it to report both mean and median.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Splitting into columns







separate_wider_delim()


A time like "11:30 pm" has two pieces separated by a space. This function splits a column on a delimiter, with a new column per piece. You supply names for the new columns.



















It refuses to guess


separate_wider_delim() expects every string to split into the same number of pieces. Real data does not. The function errors rather than guessing, and the message tells you what to try.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Debug mode
too_few = "debug" and too_many = "debug" keep the result but add diagnostic columns, named after the input column:

bedtime_ok: did this row split cleanly?
bedtime_pieces: how many pieces it had
bedtime_remainder: any leftover text










Too few pieces: 11:30PM, 2330, midnight
Too many pieces: around 11 pm, no set time, and entries with a stray space at the start

Fixing it
Tidy first, then tell the function what to do:

str_trim() removes stray spaces at the start and end
str_to_lower() makes PM, Pm and pm the same
too_few = "align_start" fills missing pieces with NA at the end
too_many = "merge" glues the extra pieces onto the last column

section: Can we make the chart readable?
text:
Can we make the chart readable?
Here is what the pipeline gives us without any work:









Programs are in alphabetical order, which tells me nothing








Definition


A factor is how R stores a categorical variable that has a fixed set of possible values, which is called levels. Factors let you choose the order.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Creating a factor







factor()


Strings sort alphabetically (in default), which is rarely what you want. Start with a list of valid levels, then pass it to factor():



















Silent NA


Any value that is not in levels silently becomes NA. There is no warning. Always check the result.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reordering levels







fct_reorder()


This function fct_reorder(f, x) orders the levels of f by the values in x. It is perfect for plots.













The program that sleeps the least is at the bottom, the most at the top

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reordering by hand







fct_relevel()


The “sleep groups” from Lecture 8 are text, so a plot puts them in alphabetical order. fct_relevel() lets you list the levels in the order you want.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Renaming levels







fct_recode()


This function can be used to rename a level. The syntax is new name = "old name". Also, levels you do not mention stay the same.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Merging levels







fct_collapse()


This function can combine levels and put them into groups. In this case, we want to group the drinks by how much caffeine they usually contain:



















A lookup table is better


Typing groupings by hand is fine for five drinks. With many levels, you would use a lookup table with the caffeine amounts instead. That is a join, in Lecture 11.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:

Numbers gave us the averages, the hours and minutes
Strings gave us the label
Factors gave us the order

Aesthetics at a glance



Aesthetic
Controls
Mapping example




x, y
position
aes(x = displ, y = hwy)


color
outline / point color
aes(color = class)


fill
interior color (bars, areas)
aes(fill = class)


shape
point symbol (≤6 levels)
aes(shape = drv)


size
point/line size (continuous only)
aes(size = cty)


alpha
transparency (continuous only)
aes(alpha = year)









Important


Inside aes() = mapping, which is driven by data and you get a legend.
Outside aes()= setting, which is essentially a fixed constant, no legend.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mapping vs. setting







Mapping


Ties an aesthetic to a variable in your data. The value changes per row, and ggplot2 draws a legend. Written inside aes().











Setting


Gives an aesthetic one fixed value for every point, no matter what the data says. No legend, since there’s nothing to decode. Written outside aes().




# Mapping: color depends on class, varies per point, gets a legend
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class))

# Setting: every point is blue, no legend
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")







Trap


geom_point(aes(color = "blue")) looks like a setting but is written inside aes(), so it’s a mapping to the constant string "blue", producing one default-palette color and a stray one-entry legend.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Stats and after_stat()
Every geom has a default stat that computes what actually gets plotted. For geom_bar(), that default is count: the number of rows in each group. You never have to ask for it explicitly.







after_stat()


Lets you reach into the stat’s output and ask for a different computed variable instead of the default:



Variable
Definition




count
number of observations per group (default)


prop
proportion of the total each group represents


density
count standardized so the area under the curve sums to 1








ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = after_stat(prop), group = 1)) + geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Count vs. proportion vs. density
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "count (default)")
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = after_stat(prop), group = 1)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "prop")
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500) +
  labs(title = "density")



















Note


Same data, same bars, three different y-axes. count shows raw group sizes; prop rescales so every bar’s height reflects its share of the whole (summing to 1 across bars); density is more commonly used with histograms/freqpolys and re-scales for area rather than height, here it looks nearly identical to prop since geom_bar() bins are all width 1.

The distinction







Variation


How much a single variable’s values differ from one observation to the next.











Covariation


The tendency for two or more variables to move together. If two variables covary, knowing one improves your guess about the other.

Categorical × categorical

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The EDA loop
EDA is not a procedure with a checklist. It’s a cycle you run until the questions stop being interesting:

Generate questions about your data
Search for answers by visualizing, transforming, and modelling
Refine your questions, or generate new ones from what you found

Most of what you produce during EDA gets thrown away, and that’s okay!

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Why it’s not optional







Important note


Dead ends are expected and not failure.




Even when the research question arrives fully formed, you still have to know whether the data can answer it.







Data cleaning


A special case of EDA: you’re asking whether the data meets your expectations, and using the same tools like visualization, transformation, modelling to find out.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two Guiding Questions

What variation occurs within my variables?
What covariation occurs between my variables?








Variation


How much a single variable’s values differ from one observation to the next. Even measuring the same quantity repeatedly gives slightly different results, and real differences between subjects or across time add even more spread.











Covariation


The tendency for two or more variables to move together. If two variables covary, knowing the value of one improves your guess about the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A simple example
Weigh 10 apples from the same tree:
142g, 138g, 151g, 145g, 149g, 133g, 156g, 144g, 140g, 147g
That spread, some apples heavier, some lighter, is variation: natural differences within one variable, even from apples off the same tree.
Now also measure each apple’s diameter:



Diameter (cm)
Weight (g)




6.5
133


7.0
140


7.8
151


8.1
156



Bigger diameter tends to mean more weight. The two variables move together, that’s covariation. Knowing one lets you make a real guess about the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Variation







Variation


The tendency of a variable’s values to change from one measurement to thenext.





Even a perfectly constant quantity will read slightly differently each time you measure it. That’s measurement noise.
Real variables also differ between subjects and over time on top of that noise, and the combination gives every variable its own characteristic shape.
Some cluster tightly, some spread wide, some have several common values.
You can’t see that shape in a long column of numbers. Plotting the distribution is how you see it.

text:
The Diamond Data



Variable
Meaning




price
price in US dollars


carat
weight of the diamond


cut
quality of the cut: Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal


color
diamond color, from J (worst) to D (best)


clarity
how clear the diamond is: I1 (worst) to IF (best)


x, y, z
length, width, depth in mm

A first look

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)

Changing the Binwidth

ggplot(smaller, aes(x = carat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)


Same data. A much narrower bin reveals structure the first plot hid entirely.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Typical values: what to ask







Checkpoint



Which values are most common? Why?
Which are rare? Does that match what you expected?
What are the gaps?
Are there unexpected patterns? What could explain them?





For the carat histogram: why the spikes at whole carats and common fractions? And why more diamonds just above each spike than just below?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Clusters mean subgroups
When a distribution separates into clumps, you can ask yourself:

How are observations within a cluster alike?
How do clusters differ from each other?
What explains the split?
Could the clusters be an artifact rather than real structure?








Recall from last week


The three clusters from Financial Wellness data: stressed, coping, and comfortable.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Unusual values hide in plain sight
text:
Unusual values hide in plain sight

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)


The only hint of anything odd is how wide the x-axis is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Zoom in on the y-axis

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Zooming In
Now three unusual regions show up: near 0, around 30, and around 60.







coord_cartesian()


The bars are still computed from all the data, so you can safely zoom the y-axis to see rare bins without changing what got counted.
ylim()/xlim() instead discard any data outside the limits before the stat runs, which can silently change your bar heights.
When you just want a closer look, reach for coord_cartesian().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Outliers
A value that sits far away from the rest of a variable’s values, unusual enough that it stands out from the general pattern. Outliers can come from a few different places:







A real, unusual observation


The value is correct. It just represents something genuinely rare, an extremely large diamond, an exceptionally tall person.











A measurement or data entry error


The value is wrong. A typo, a broken sensor, a missing value coded as 0 instead of NA. This is common and worth checking first.











Why they matter


An outlier can quietly distort summaries like the mean or a fitted trend line, so it’s worth investigating rather than ignoring. But it should never be dropped automatically just because it’s inconvenient, understanding why it’s unusual comes first.




You can’t always spot an outlier from a column of numbers. Plotting the distribution, and sometimes zooming in, is usually what reveals it.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Pull the outliers out

unusual <- diamonds |>
  filter(y < 3 | y > 20) |>
  select(price, x, y, z) |>
  arrange(y)

unusual

# A tibble: 9 × 4
  price     x     y     z
  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  5139  0      0    0   
2  6381  0      0    0   
3 12800  0      0    0   
4 15686  0      0    0   
5 18034  0      0    0   
6  2130  0      0    0   
7  2130  0      0    0   
8  2075  5.15  31.8  5.12
9 12210  8.09  58.9  8.06

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What we found
y is a dimension in millimeters. A diamond cannot be 0 mm wide, so those are missing data encoded as zero.

You wouldn’t have been able to find these simply by searching for NA as missing data.

The 32 mm and 59 mm entries are implausible too!






Important


This is the core payoff of EDA: visualizing the data surfaced a data-quality problem that a search for NA never would have. Always sanity-check units and physically-plausible ranges, not just missingness flags.









Caution


Run your analysis with and without the outliers. If it barely moves and you can’t explain them, dropping them is defensible. If it moves a lot, find the cause and disclose the removal in your write-up — don’t drop values without justification just because they’re inconvenient.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two ways to handle them

# Option 1: drop the whole row — usually too blunt
diamonds2 <- diamonds |> filter(between(y, 3, 20))

# Option 2: replace the bad value with NA — usually better
diamonds2 <- diamonds |>
  mutate(y = if_else(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))







Note


filter() basically isolates the rows where the y values are between 3 and 20, while keeping the rest of the variables (as long as their corresponding y is between 3 and 20). It discards the rest.
mutate() changes (like mutation) the column of y such that if y is less than 3 OR y is greater than 20, then the corresponding y value becomes NA.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing values in plots
ggplot2 won’t guess where to put an NA, so it drops them and warns you. Silence the warning with na.rm = TRUE (only once you’ve understood why they’re missing).

diamonds2 <- diamonds |> mutate(y = if_else(y < 3 | y > 20, NA, y))

ggplot(diamonds2, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 9 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

Try it yourself



Explore the distributions of x, y, and z in diamonds. Which is length, which width, which depth?
Explore price. Try a wide range of binwidths. Anything surprising?
How many diamonds are 0.99 carat vs. exactly 1 carat? Why the gap?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Covariation
If variation describes behavior within a variable, covariation describes behavior between variables: the tendency for two or more variables to move together.
The strategy depends on the variable types:

categorical × numerical
categorical × categorical
numerical × numerical

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Categorical × numerical:

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75)









The Count Problem


Group sizes differ so much that shape differences are invisible. Do you think each cut share the same pattern?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Switch the y-axis to density
Density is the count standardized so the area under each curve is 1. Since it isn’t a column in the data, after_stat() fetches it from the stat. The following plot is a frequency polygon.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(color = cut), binwidth = 500, linewidth = 0.75)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Frequency polygons vs Boxplots
Fair diamonds (the lowest quality cut) appear to have the highest average price.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reordering
cut is an ordered factor, so its order is meaningful. Most categorical variables aren’t.







Ordered Cuts


It goes from Fair -> Good -> Very Good -> Premium -> Ideal.











What do you do if the categories are: Apples, Oranges, Bananas?


This fct_reorder(variable, by, fun) function sorts factor levels by a summary statistic (e.g. mean/median) of another variable, which almost always makes a categorical-vs-numeric plot easier to read at a glance.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Example
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median), y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Flip when labels are long
Swap the x and y mappings with no extra function needed:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy, y = fct_reorder(class, hwy, median))) +
  geom_boxplot()

Categorical × categorical: counts

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = color)) +
  geom_count()


Circle area shows how many observations fall at each combination.

Would you argue that there is a lot of overplotting in this figure?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Interrogating a pattern
A systematic relationship shows up as a pattern. When you spot one, try and ask yourself:

Could this be coincidence?
How would you describe the relationship?
How strong is it?
What other variables might be involved?
Does it hold within subgroups?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Variation vs. covariation
Variation is uncertainty within a single variable. If price varies a lot on its own, knowing nothing else, you can’t say much about what a given diamond costs. Covariation between variables cuts that uncertainty down.






Tip


If carat and price covary, then knowing a diamond’s carat narrows down your guess for its price a lot more than guessing blind. The stronger the covariation, the more one variable tells you about the other.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Modelling
This is the entire logic behind prediction and modelling: a useful predictor is just a variable that covaries with the outcome you care about. A variable that doesn’t covary with the outcome is useless as a predictor, no matter how interesting it looks on its own.

E.g. income with financial wellness








Correlation does not imply causation?


Covariation is not the same as causation. Two variables can covary because one causes the other, because both are driven by a third variable, or by pure coincidence.

E.g. The divorce rate in Maine correlates with per capita margarine consumption

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summary

EDA is a loop:

ask questions
→ visualize/transform/model
→ formualte better questions

Variation within a variable: typical values, clusters, unusual values
Outliers are sometimes errors, sometimes discoveries. Investigate before deciding; disclose what you removed.
Covariation between variables: pick the technique by variable type

Next: turning exploratory graphics into ones other people can read.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Before we look at the raw data…
text:
Before we look at the raw data…







Thinking Moment


What do you think could go wrong with real, raw survey data?











Potential Problems


What kinds of problems might it have that yesterday’s polished plots didn’t show?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Here’s the actual raw file

survey_2017_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2017.csv")

# Note the skip = 1 -- 2022's file has a stray metadata line above the
# real header (a leftover from the export on the new survey platform)
survey_2022_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2022.csv", skip = 1)

glimpse(survey_2017_raw)
glimpse(survey_2022_raw)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Duplicate responses (rows)
A few respondents show up more than once. - Think of this as a double-submitted survey.

survey_2017_raw |> count(respondent_id, sort = TRUE) |> filter(n > 1)

survey_2017_raw <- survey_2017_raw |> distinct()
survey_2022_raw <- survey_2022_raw |> distinct()


The function distinct() removes exact duplicate rows. It is always worth checking for before doing anything else), since duplicates quietly inflate every count.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Tidy data: benefits are stuck in wide format

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions







The format for income response is a mess!


Sometimes people are allowed to type in their responses however they like. For example, if someone has an annual income of $85,000, there are several ways they might enter that in the survey:

"85000"
"$85,000"
"85,000"
"85K"

So how do we take all these different formats and turn them into something we can actually work with in our analysis?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Recall from last week’s survey
For Question 7 of the survey, I asked everyone what was the best sandwich?







Most Popular Answer


Grilled Cheese was among the most popular answers. But this is what I got from last week’s survey response:

Grilled cheese
Grilled Cheese
Grilled Cheese!
grilled cheese
grilled cheese with Hot sauce
Grilled cheese sandwich
Ham Grilled Cheese

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions: provinces
Same province, several spellings: "Ontario", "ON", "ontario ".

standardize_province <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower()
  case_when(
    x %in% c("ontario", "on") ~ "Ontario",
    x %in% c("alberta", "ab") ~ "Alberta",
    x %in% c("british columbia", "bc") ~ "British Columbia",
    x %in% c("quebec", "qc") ~ "Quebec",
    TRUE ~ str_to_title(x)
  )
}

survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province))
survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Strings & expressions: Yes/No
We might get three variations for the same two answers: "Yes"/"No", "Y"/"N", "yes"/"no".

standardize_yn <- function(x) {
  x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower()
  case_when(
    x %in% c("yes", "y") ~ "Yes",
    x %in% c("no", "n") ~ "No",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
}

survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed))
survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Missing data







Where did missing data come from?


Sometimes we don’t always get all the complete data set that we want.

People tend to skip questions that they don’t feel comfortable answer.
perhaps people forgot to fill in one of the questions/pages of survey.
maybe people gave some weird looking answer that is unusable (e.g $*@2#$1aE&)
or sometimes these questions are simply irrelevant to them

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two options: 1) Delete the row
If a respondent didn’t answer a question in the survey, we can just remove this person entirely from the data analysis. :)







This is cool, but…


While this is a simple method, you will lose the respondents.

if the people who skipped the question aren’t random, the ones left behind don’t represent everyone fairly.






survey_2017_nomiss <- survey_2017_clean |>
  drop_na(income, savings_pct,
          debt_overwhelmed,
          emergency_fund_likelihood)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Two options: 2) Imputation
Instead of throwing the whole response away, we can guess a reasonable value to put in its place.

like using the average of everyone else’s answer. (e.g. mean or median)


survey_2017_clean |> mutate(income = ifelse(is.na(income), median(income, na.rm = TRUE), income))








This is cool, but…


Now some of your “data” is really just a guess. If you fill in too many values this way, your data can look more similar than it actually is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mismatched response







Too many response levels


Sometimes survey designers choose a set of response options one year, then decide to change them the next. For example, in our financial wellness data, the survey asked questions of How difficult is it to obtain $2,000 of emergency fund?:

in 2017, there are 7 levels: Very difficult, Difficult, Somewhat difficult, Neither, Somewhat manageable, Manageable, Very manageable
in 2022, there are now only 5 levels: Very difficult, Difficult, Neither, Manageable, Very manageable

So what do you do? Neither of them directly match each other. And this is difficult for a year-to-year comparative analysis

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Potential Solution







Compromise


We can collapse both down to 3 levels — Difficult, Neither, Manageable.





survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when(
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult", "Somewhat difficult") ~ "Difficult",
    emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither",
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Somewhat manageable", "Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |>
  mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when(
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult") ~ "Difficult",
    emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither",
    emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Before: 7 Levels vs 5 Levels

Different number of categories, different wording. It is not easy to tell how people have changed over time by comparing these two bar plots side by side as-is.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
After:

Now that both years use the same 3 levels, we can finally put them side by side and ask: did things get better, worse, or stay the same?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Different ways of asking the same question
text:
Different ways of asking the same question







Mismatched question: same question, different name


Sometimes a question gets worded differently across years, even though it’s really asking the same thing.

in 2017, the survey asked How difficult was it for you if your paycheque is delayed?

stored as paycheque_delay_difficulty

in 2022, the question became If there is a two week delay in your paycheque arrival, how impactful would it be to your finances?

stored as twoweek_pay_delay_impact


Same underlying question, different wording and different column name — rename() fixes this in one line each.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mismatched responses: Age

survey_2017_clean |> select(age) |> head()
survey_2022_clean |> select(age) |> head()








Are you willing to share your age?


Sometimes the same underlying question gets measured differently across years, even when the intent is identical.

in 2017, respondents gave an exact age

stored as age, e.g. 34

in 2022, respondents picked from age brackets instead

stored as age, e.g. "30-40"

Now we have the same underlying question, but a different level of precision

In order to compare over the years, everyone needs to speak the same bucket language.







survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(age_bucket = case_when(
    age <= 30 ~ "18-30",
    age <= 40 ~ "30-40",
    age <= 50 ~ "40-50",
    age <= 65 ~ "50-65",
    TRUE ~ "65+"
  ))

survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |>
  rename(age_bucket = age)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Removed benefit option: aligning categories







Non-existent Option in Survey


“Educational funding” existed as a choice in 2017, but the 2022 platform dropped it. To compare years fairly, we fold anything not offered in both years into a shared “Other” category.





survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |>
  mutate(benefit_preference = if_else(
    benefit_preference == "benefit_education",
    "benefit_other",
    benefit_preference
  ))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Combine into one data set

survey_combined <- bind_rows(survey_2017_clean, survey_2022_clean)

glimpse(survey_combined)








Only possible now


Now that we have:
— column names match (rename()) - category sets match (the “Other” recoded) - response scales match (the 3-level of likert responses in paycheque question)
Every fix so far existed to make this one line possible.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Too much info in one column
text:
Too much info in one column







One column doing two jobs


The variable respondent_id looks like a single value, but it’s actually smuggling in two separate pieces of information at once.

the year the response came from, e.g. 2017
the respondent’s number within that year, e.g. 0001

Both are jammed into one string: "2017-0001". If we ever want to work with just the year, or just the respondent number, we’re stuck first pulling them apart.





survey_combined <- survey_combined |>
  separate(respondent_id, into = c("survey_year", "respondent_num"), sep = "-")

survey_combined |>
  select(survey_year, respondent_num, everything()) |>
  head()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Show concluding results

survey_combined |>
  ggplot(aes(x = financial_wellness_cluster, y = income, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) +
  labs(title = "Income by Cluster: 2017 vs 2022",
       x = "Cluster", y = "Income ($)", fill = "Year") +
  theme_minimal()


This is the exact plot style from Day 1, except now you’ve watched every step of how the data underneath it got here.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Back to your predictions







Discussion


Which of your guesses from the start of class came true?
What did we run into that nobody predicted?











Document your decisions


A results plot without its cleaning log is a claim without evidence. For any real report, this deserves its own short section (ahem your final report):

Which rows/columns were dropped, and why
Every recoding decision (e.g. collapsing levels and combining buckets, etc.)
What’s imputed vs. observed, clearly marked

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
A few cautions







Keep in mind



Every cleaning choice was also an analytical choice — a different 3-level collapse, a different age-bucket rule, a different imputation method could all shift what we find downstream
This dataset is synthetic: today’s numbers are illustrative, not a claim about real Canadians
Later this semester: missing-data methods and statistical tests that let you make these calls more rigorously than by eyeballing

What are missing values?









Explicit missing
Implicit missing




Idea

A simple example















Checkpoint


What is the missing data here?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Example Continued

Tuesday is explicit: the row exists and n is NA
Wednesday is implicit: there is no row at all








Plots hide implicit gaps


A chart of this table draws Mon, Tue, Thu. Nothing on the plot says that Wednesday is missing.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:

Imputation







Definition


Imputation means filling in a missing value with an estimate.

Fixed value: a number you choose, such as 0
Mean: the average of the answers we have (mean imputation)
Last value: the last known value above it












It comes with a cost


Filling with the mean keeps the average but shrinks the spread (sd), and it makes 35 students look more typical than they are. Dropping rows loses students. There is no free option, so choose, and say which.

complete()


This function adds the rows that are missing from a table. You tell it which values should exist, and it creates a row for every one that’s absent, and fill the other columns with NA or a value that you choose.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics

Keys







Primary Key


A primary key is a column whose values are unique: no two rows share one, so each value picks out exactly one row. E.g.

student_id in survey: each ID is one student
The drink column in the drinks table: “Coffee” appears in one row only












Foreign Key


A foreign key is a column in another table that holds those same values. - favourite_drink in survey holds drink names like “Coffee” - Many students can share the same favourite drink like coffee

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Combining tables







left_join()


The function left_join(x, y) keeps every row of x and adds the matching columns of y. In the end, you will get the same number of rows but more columns (more information you learn about each observation).

You can also use join_by(a == b) to say which column in x matches with which column in y

Contains some basic functions and visualization tools.

Initializing R packages

Use install.packages("package_name") in the console to install R packages on your own machine.

Example: install.packages("ggplot2") to install ggplot2.

Use library(package_name) to initialize already installed packages.

Example: library(ggplot2) to load ggplot2.

To install the package if it isn’t already installed and then initialize it after installation:

if(!require(package_name)) install.packages("package_name")
library(package_name)

Assigning Variables

The operators =, <-, and -> can be used to assign values to variables

If we want to assign x = 2; x=2, x<-2, and 2->x are equivalent.
Common convention is to use <- but feel free to use =.

Rules for variable names.

Start with a letter (x5 is OK but 5x is NOT.)
Consist of letters, numbers, underscores, and periods (x_5 and x.5 are OK but not x-5).
Case sensitive (x and X would be different variables).

Variable naming conventions

Try to use meaningful names.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Displaying Output

R will display the outputs of unassigned calculations

exp(3) would compute \(e^3\) (approximately) and display the result.

R suppresses the output of assigned calculations

x<-exp(3) would compute \(e^3\) and store the result in x but would not display anything.
To see that value of x we would need to run print(x) or just x.

Use rm() to remove objects from the current workspace.

The call rm(x,y,z) will remove the variables x, y, and z from the workspace.
The call rm(list=ls()) will remove all objects from the workspace.
The workspace is automatically cleared when RStudio is exited.

What’s the take-away message from the plot above (labelled Figure 2)?

 The blue team always wins. If you score 4 goals, you're guaranteed to win. Scoring more goals than the other team only has a slight correlation with winning the game. Taking more shots has a very slight correlation with scoring more goals.

Figure 2 used veritcal jittering for the number of goals. Why?

 for display purposes. The jittering is done because goals is a continuous variable but was only measured to the nearest whole number; jittering makes it continuous rather than discrete. This jittering is inapproriate - it implies that there were games with 4.2 goals which is impossible. Since goals are whole numbers, all games with, say, 20 shots and 4 goals will be plotted in the exact same spot. Jittering allows us to see this.

From the plot above (Figure 2), how many shots do you need to take in order to have more than a 50% chance to win the game?

 20 40 60 It is impossible to tell from this plot.


In Figure 2, does it appear that shooting more makes you more likely to win?


Answer

Not really! As you take more shots you get more goals, but perhaps your opponent shoots more as well. If you look at, say, 20 shots in a game, it looks like slightly more than half of the games were won. If you look at 40 shots, it still looks like slightly more than half of the games were won.
It really matters what the opponent does!



What is the interpretation of the plot above (Figure 3)?

 The number of shots is uncorrelated with whether the team wins - it's still a 50-50 chance. There's more variation at the extremes because there were fewer games with that number of shots. The overall chance of winning is not exactly 50% because very few of the values are actually 50%. This plot shows how many games a team won at each number of shots. If a team takes 60 shots, they are guaranteed to lose, but if they take exactly 55 shots they have a 75% chance of winning. During a game, a team should stop shooting when they hit 55 shots.

You plot City Mileage (cty) vs. Highway Mileage (hwy) for 234 cars using geom_point(). When you look at the plot, you only see about 100 dots. What is happening, and why is this plot misleading?

 Multiple cars have identical rounded mileage values, causing their points to land on exact same coordinates and stack directly on top of each other. Over half of the cars in the dataset have missing mileage values. geom_point() only plots a random sample of the data when datasets exceed 100 rows. Cars with identical highway and city mileage automatically cancel each other out on the graph.

I created a histogram of continuous highway gas mileage (hwy) using geom_histogram(). By default, ggplot2 uses 30 bins and displays a warning suggesting that the user pick a better binwidth. What happens to the story the plot tells if the student sets an extremely small bin width (e.g., binwidth = 0.1) versus an extremely large bin width (e.g., binwidth = 20)?

 An extremely small bin width converts the plot into a boxplot; an extremely large bin width converts it into a scatterplot. An extremely small bin width only plots outliers; an extremely large bin width only plots the median. ggplot2 automatically rejects bin widths smaller than 1.0 with a fatal error. An extremely small bin width creates too much visual noise (individual spikes), while an extremely large bin width over-smooths the data and hides features like bimodality or skewness.

Choosing How to Show Data







Quick distinctions



Continuous: a numeric value that can (in theory) take any value in a range.
Categorical: falls into one of several unordered groups (nominal) or has only two options (binary).
Likert: an ordered scale (e.g., “very difficult” → “difficult” → … → “very manageable”)

categorical, but with a meaningful order.













One idea to hold onto


The type of variable decides the type of plot.

One category at a time → bar chart
One number at a time → histogram
Two things at once → scatterplot (or boxplot, if one is a category)

Where we are
In this week, I will give you a working template for plots. This chapter explains why that template works.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)

We’ll work mostly with two datasets that ship with ggplot2:

mpg — 234 car models, 11 variables
diamonds — ~54,000 diamonds


mpg |> select(manufacturer, model, displ, hwy, class, drv) |> head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  manufacturer model displ   hwy class   drv  
  <chr>        <chr> <dbl> <int> <chr>   <chr>
1 audi         a4      1.8    29 compact f

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Data
Every ggplot() call starts with the same first argument: a data frame (or tibble).

ggplot(data = mpg) +
  geom_point(aes(x = displ, y = hwy))

mpg fills in <DATA> from the template. Nothing gets drawn until ggplot2 knows which data frame to pull the variables displ and hwy out of the mappings in aes().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Data can change per layer
ggplot(data = ...) sets the default data for every layer. Any geom can override it with its own data argument:

ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = mpg |> filter(class == "2seater"), color = "red")

The first layer inherits mpg from ggplot(); the second layer supplies its own filtered data frame instead. Same idea you’ll see again in the Layers section:

data is a slot you can fill once globally, or override locally.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The pipe: |>
The symbol |> takes what’s on its left and feeds it in as the first argument of the function on its right.

mpg |> select(manufacturer, model, displ, hwy)

# is exactly the same as:
select(mpg, manufacturer, model, displ, hwy)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Analogy







If you like math…


Think of a two-variable function \(f(x, y)\).
The pipe works like plugging a value in for one of the arguments. Piping 5 into \(y\) gives you \(f(x, 5)\). Essentially you’ve fixed one input and left the rest open.











Connecting back to coding


When we write mpg |> filter(...) |> select(...), we’re doing the same thing: treating mpg like the input we’re plugging in, and filter(...), select(...) like functions waiting to receive it as their first argument.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Mapping a variable to an aesthetic
text:
Mapping a variable to an aesthetic
An aesthetic is a visual property of the marks on the plot: position, color, shape, size, transparency.
aes() says “let this variable control that property.”

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Not every aesthetic suits
You can change the shape of scatterplots from circles to triangles, stars, squares, etc.
But shape only supplies six distinct symbols before it gives up: the seventh category simply goes unplotted, with a warning.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = class)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: The shape palette can deal with a maximum of 6 discrete values because more
than 6 becomes difficult to discriminate
ℹ you have requested 7 values. Consider specifying shapes manually if you need
  that many of them.


Warning: Removed 62 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Problems with shape levels






Warning


class has seven levels but shape can only display six. SUVs (62 rows) silently disappear from the plot above. You should always read the warnings ggplot2 gives you, they’re telling you data went missing from the picture.




ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Point customization







Checkpoint


What do you think size and alpha does?





size changes the size of the dot (smaller-larger)
alpha changes the transparency of the dot (lighter-darker)
These two aesthetics are ranked.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Ordered aesthetics

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = class)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Using size for a discrete variable is not advised.










Mapping an unordered category


class (e.g. 2seater, compact, midsize, …) has no inherent order. Mapping it to size or alpha visually implies “bigger/darker = more,” which is misleading for a purely categorical variable. Save these aesthetics for variables that are genuinely ordered or continuous.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Mapping vs. setting
Inside aes() = mapping, driven by data, gets a legend. Outside aes() = setting, a fixed constant, no legend.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 2, shape = 17)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Setting values
When you set an aesthetic you supply a raw value:



Aesthetic
Value




color
colour name "blue" or hex string "#E81B23"


size
point size in mm, size = 1


shape
an integer 0–25, shape = 1


alpha
opacity from 0 to 1



Shapes 0–14 are hollow (border from color), 15–20 are solid (filled with color), and 21–25 take both a color border and a fill.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



Draw hwy vs. displ with pink filled triangles.
Why does the code below not produce blue points?
What happens with aes(color = displ < 5)?





ggplot(mpg) +
  geom_point(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = "blue"))

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: A geom is how the data gets drawn
text:
A geom is how the data gets drawn
Same data, same mappings, different geom:



ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point()










ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_smooth()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Geoms accept different aesthetics
A line has no shape; a point has no linetype. ggplot2 quietly ignores aesthetics a geom can’t use.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, linetype = drv)) +
  geom_smooth()


Mapping a discrete variable splits the geom into one object per level.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Grouping without a legend
group splits the data the same way, but adds no legend and no visual distinction.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = drv))








Note


group is what mapping a discrete variable does implicitly behind the scenes. You should use it when you want the splitting behaviour without the legend or the visual distinction that color or linetype would add.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Layers stack
Multiple geoms in one plot. Mappings in ggplot() are global; mappings in a geom are local to that layer.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Layers can have their own data
text:
Layers can have their own data
Useful for highlighting a subset:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(
    data = mpg |> filter(class == "2seater"),
    color = "red", size = 2
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Different geoms
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) + geom_density()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()













The histogram and density show bimodality and right skew; the boxplot compresses that into a summary but flags outliers.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Common geoms at a glance








Chart type
Geom
What it draws




Line chart
geom_line()
Connects points in order of the x-value — good for trends over a continuous sequence (e.g. time)


Bar plot
geom_bar()
Counts observations per category and draws bar height as the count (uses stat_count())


Bar plot (pre-counted)
geom_col()
Bar height comes directly from a y column you already have — no counting


Histogram
geom_histogram()
Bins a continuous variable and draws bar height as the count per bin


Boxplot
geom_boxplot()
Five-number summary (min, Q1, median, Q3, max) plus outliers, per group


Area chart
geom_area()
Like geom_line(), but fills the region under the line

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Boxplots
A boxplot summarizes a distribution with five numbers: the minimum, the first quartile (Q1), the median, the third quartile (Q3), and the maximum. Points far from the rest get drawn separately as individual outliers.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Reading a boxplot







What each part means



The box spans Q1 to Q3, the middle 50% of the data (the interquartile range, or IQR).
The line inside the box is the median.
The whiskers extend to the farthest point still within 1.5 times the IQR from the box.
Dots beyond the whiskers are flagged as outliers.











Tip


A boxplot is a compression. It tells you center and spread at a glance, but it can’t show you whether a group has one peak or several, since all of that shape detail gets collapsed into five numbers.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Violin plots
A violin plot replaces the box with a mirrored density curve, so you see the full shape of the distribution instead of just a summary.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_violin()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Boxplot vs. violin plot
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) + geom_boxplot()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) + geom_violin()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Boxplot vs violin plot






Important


Use a boxplot when you mainly care about comparing medians and spread across many groups at once, it stays compact even with a dozen categories side by side.
Use a violin plot when the shape itself matters, for example spotting bimodal groups, since a boxplot cannot distinguish “spread out evenly” from “two separate clusters.”









Caution


Violin plots need enough points per group to draw a reliable density curve. With a small group, the “shape” you see may just be noise from too few observations, not a real pattern.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Try out different plots






Try it yourself



Which geom draws a line chart? A boxplot? A histogram? An area chart?
What does show.legend = FALSE do, and why might you want it?
Try uncommenting different sections below to see how each chart type behaves with 1 vs. 2 variables!

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
facet_wrap(): one variable
What if we are interested in how each class of variables behave? We can split the plot into panels with one per level.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl)

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
facet_grid(): two variables
A two-sided formula, rows ~ cols.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(drv ~ cyl)


Empty panels mean that combination doesn’t occur in the data.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Free scales
By default every panel shares one scale, which is what makes panels comparable. Release that with scales:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(drv ~ cyl, scales = "free")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Free scales







Customization


"free_x", "free_y", or "free" let each row/column pick its own range.

This is easier to read within a panel, but panels are no longer directly comparable to each other.












Checkpoint


If I want to share a plot with someone that has no idea about the data set, should I use free scales or shared scales?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



What happens if you facet on a continuous variable like cty?
What does . mean in facet_grid(drv ~ .)?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Where does count come from?

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut)) +
  geom_bar()


count isn’t a column in diamonds. The geom_bar computed it.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Stats
A stat is the algorithm a geom runs on your data before drawing.

bar charts, histograms, freqpolys → bin and count
smoothers → fit a model, plot predictions
boxplots → compute a five-number summary

Every geom has a default stat; every stat has a default geom. ?geom_bar tells you it uses stat_count(), and lists the variables it computes.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Using a computed variable
after_stat() reaches into the variables the stat produced. The prop means proportion.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = after_stat(prop), group = 1)) +
  geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
group issue






Important


Without group = 1, each bar is treated as its own group and every proportion comes out as 1, then there’s nothing to divide by. Try deleting group = 1 in the live cell below and see what happens.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Calling a stat directly
Sometimes the summary is the point, and naming the stat says so:

ggplot(diamonds) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(x = cut, y = depth),
    fun.min = min, fun.max = max, fun = median
  )

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



If you swap geom_bar() for geom_col() in the plot below without changing anything else, what error (if any) do you think you’ll get? Try it and see if you were right.
Which diamond cut do you think has the smallest proportion in the data set?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
color vs. fill for bars
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, color = drv)) + geom_bar()
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, fill = drv)) + geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Stacking is a position adjustment
Map fill to a second variable and the bars stack automatically:

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, fill = class)) +
  geom_bar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The four options







Stack


"stack" — the default for bars. Segments pile on top of each other in full-height, full-count form.











Fill


"fill" — stack, then normalize each bar to the same height. Best for comparing proportions across groups, since every bar reaches 100%.











Dodge


"dodge" — segments sit side by side instead of stacking. Best for comparing individual counts directly, since bar heights stay on the original count scale.











Identity


"identity" — draws each value exactly where it falls, with no adjustment. For bars this usually means overlapping rectangles (rarely what you want); for points, it’s the default position since points have no width to adjust.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Exercise






Tip


Change position = "stack" below to "fill", "dodge", and "identity". Watch how the same data tells a different story each time.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Overplotting
hwy and displ are rounded, so points land on a grid and pile up. This scatterplot shows 126 visible points for 234 observations. The points are overlapping!

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Jittering
position = "jitter" adds a little random noise. Less accurate at small scales, far more honest at large ones.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_jitter()


geom_jitter() is shorthand for geom_point(position = "jitter").

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Your turn






Try it yourself



What’s wrong with a plain geom_point() of cty vs. hwy? Fix it below.
Is there any difference between the default and position = "identity" for points?
Try geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.5) to control the amount of jitter.
Compare geom_jitter() and geom_count().

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The default is Cartesian
x and y act independently. Two alternatives come up often enough to know:

coord_quickmap(): fixes the aspect ratio for geographic data
coord_polar(): bends the Cartesian plane into polar coordinates


nz <- map_data("nz")

ggplot(nz, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "white", color = "black") +
  coord_quickmap()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Polar coordinates
A bar chart and a Coxcomb chart are the same plot in different coordinates:
bar <- ggplot(diamonds) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = clarity, fill = clarity), show.legend = FALSE, width = 1) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)

bar + coord_flip()
bar + coord_polar()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Summary

Aesthetics map variables to visual properties; setting differs from mapping
Geoms decide how marks are drawn; layers stack and can override data and mappings
Facets split one plot into comparable panels
Stats compute the values a geom actually plots
Positions resolve overlap: stack, fill, dodge, jitter
Coordinates redefine what x and y mean

Still to come: themes, in Chapter 11 (next week).

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Where these principles come from
Not arbitrary style preferences, mostly grounded in research on how humans actually perceive and compare visual information.






Note


The preferred visualization choices are the ones that best match how our brains process shapes, lengths, and positions, not just what looks nice.










Keep your goal in mind


A plot for yourself during exploration will look different from a plot built to communicate a finding to an audience.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
section: Not all visual cues are equal
text:
Not all visual cues are equal
Several visual channels are available to represent a value: position, length, angle, area, brightness, colour hue.







Human’s perception


We are quite good at comparing position and length. We are noticeably worse at judging angles, and even worse at judging area alone. Brightness and colour hue are the hardest of all to quantify precisely.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Can you read pie charts?
A pie chart encodes each value with both angle and area simultaneously.
ggplot(browsers |> filter(year == "2000"), aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = browser)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) + coord_polar("y") +
  labs(title = "2000", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_void()
ggplot(browsers |> filter(year == "2015"), aes(x = "", y = pct, fill = browser)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) + coord_polar("y") +
  labs(title = "2015", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_void()

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
What about bar plots?

ggplot(browsers, aes(x = fct_reorder(browser, pct, .fun = mean), y = pct, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = seq(0, 30, 10), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Browser", y = "Percent", fill = "Year",
       title = "Browser share is far easier to compare as a barplot")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Length implies proportionality

When a visual cue is length (as in a bar plot), the reader assumes the length is proportional to the value.
If the bar doesn’t start at 0, that assumption breaks and a small real difference can be stretched to look huge.








Common problem in media


This is a favourite trick of misleading charts in the media: truncate the y-axis, and a 16% increase can be made to look like it nearly tripled.

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text: Exaggerated axis truncation

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
How to exaggerate an increase?







Try playing around with the axis


The template below compares my company’s profit in 2011 and 2012. Notice how much bigger the increase looks once the y-axis gets truncated. Which plot would you rather show?

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
Length vs Position
ggplot(life_exp, aes(x = continent, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 85)) +
  labs(title = "Forced to include 0")
ggplot(life_exp, aes(x = continent, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Zoomed to the data")

title: DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics
text:
The rule of thumb







Is the 0 required here?


The empty space between 0 and 50 in the left plot adds no information and makes it harder to see the within-group and between-group variability that actually matters here.











Bars vs Points


If length is your visual cue (bars), always include 0. If position is your cue (points, lines), it’s fine (often better) to zoom to the range that matters.

Radius-proportional vs. area-proportional
















Tip


ggplot2’s scale_size_area() defaults to making area, not radius, proportional to the value — the mathematically honest choice. Worth knowing which default you’re getting when you map a value to size.

Jitter and alpha blending
Two small fixes make an enormous difference when points overlap heavily:







Jitter

geom_jitter(width=...) adjusts the amount of horizontal jitter.












Alpha


Does anyone recall what does alpha change to a plot?
